parts.label: (a)
hints: Hint 1: Think about what a wave model would predict - if light were only a continuous wave spreading energy, how should brighter light and waiting longer affect electrons?
Hint 2: Focus on how the observations split into two separate roles - what controls how energetic each electron is, compared with what controls how many electrons come out per second?
Hint 3: Remember the two most surprising timing and frequency clues - is there a cut-off frequency, and is there any delay before emission starts?
parts.proper_answer: Any three from: max KE of electrons depends on frequency, not intensity; rate of emission depends on intensity at constant frequency; threshold frequency below which no emission; instantaneous emission with no time delay.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Why Wave Theory Fails**
Think of light as a wave spreading energy continuously. Brighter light should give more energetic electrons, any frequency should eventually work if you wait long enough, and there should be a time delay while energy builds up. None of this is observed, so we need particles.

Step 2: **Energy Comes in Packets**
In the photon picture, one photon hits one electron in a one-to-one interaction with energy $$E = hf$$. So the maximum energy of the emitted electron depends on frequency $f$, not on intensity. Increasing intensity only increases the number of photons, so it increases the rate of emission, not the energy of each electron.

Step 3: **Threshold and Instant Action**
If $$hf$$ is less than the work function $\Phi$, no electron can escape, giving a threshold frequency $f_0$ below which there is zero emission whatever the intensity. Since energy arrives in a concentrated packet, absorption is instantaneous with no delay.

parts.label: (b)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Start by thinking about what determines the energy of a single packet of light - which two universal constants link that energy to the given wavelength?
Hint 2: Use $$E = hc/\lambda$$ with $\lambda = 380 \text{ nm} = 380 \times 10^{-9} \text{ m}$ to find $E$ in joules.
Hint 3: Convert your joule answer to electronvolts by dividing by $1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J eV}^{-1}$ and give 2 or 3 s.f.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Photon Energy From Wavelength**
A photon of frequency $f$ and wavelength $\lambda$ carries energy $$E = hf = \frac{hc}{\lambda}$$ where $h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \text{ J s}$ and $c = 3.0 \times 10^{8} \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

Step 2: **Calculate in Joules**
Convert wavelength to metres: $$\lambda = 380 \text{ nm} = 380 \times 10^{-9} \text{ m}$$ Then $$E = \frac{(6.63 \times 10^{-34})(3.0 \times 10^{8})}{380 \times 10^{-9}}$$ $$E = 5.23 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J}$$

Step 3: **Convert to Electronvolts**
Since $1 \text{ eV} = 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J}$: $$E = \frac{5.23 \times 10^{-19}}{1.60 \times 10^{-19}}$$ $$E = 3.3 \text{ eV}$$ to 2 s.f.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Think about the energy budget for one electron - how does the incoming photon energy compare with the minimum energy needed to escape the metal?
Hint 2: Compare your 3.3 eV photon to each work function in Fig. 11.1 and pick out where the photon has a surplus.
parts.proper_answer: Emission requires photon energy > work function energy. $3.3 \text{ eV}$ exceeds 2.4 eV and 2.9 eV, so sodium and calcium emit photoelectrons.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Condition for Emission**
From $$hf = \Phi + K_{max}$$, an electron can only escape if the photon supplies at least the work function: $$hf > \Phi$$ If the photon energy is smaller than $\Phi$, no photoelectrons are released.

Step 2: **Apply to the Table**
Photon energy is $3.3 \text{ eV}$. Sodium $\Phi = 2.4 \text{ eV} < 3.3 \text{ eV}$ - yes. Calcium $\Phi = 2.9 \text{ eV} < 3.3 \text{ eV}$ - yes. Zinc $3.6 \text{ eV}$ and silver $4.3 \text{ eV}$ are greater than $3.3 \text{ eV}$ - no emission. So sodium and calcium only.

parts.label: (c)
key_concepts: force as rate of change of momentum
hints: Hint 1: Think in terms of momentum, not energy - when a photon is absorbed, what happens to the momentum it was carrying and what does that mean for the surface?
Hint 2: Find the momentum of one photon using $$p = h/\lambda$$ with $\lambda = 380 \times 10^{-9} \text{ m}$.
Hint 3: Link total force to the arrival rate using force = rate of change of momentum = $p \times$ number per second.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Photons Carry Momentum**
Even though photons have no mass, they carry momentum $$p = \frac{h}{\lambda}$$ When absorbed normally, each photon gives all its momentum to the surface. Force is the total momentum delivered per second.

Step 2: **Momentum of One Photon**
$$p = \frac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{380 \times 10^{-9}}$$ $$p = 1.74 \times 10^{-27} \text{ kg m s}^{-1} = 1.74 \times 10^{-27} \text{ N s}$$

Step 3: **From Rate to Force**
With $N = 7.6 \times 10^{14} \text{ s}^{-1}$ photons absorbed per second: $$F = \frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t} = Np$$ $$F = (7.6 \times 10^{14})(1.74 \times 10^{-27})$$ $$F = 1.3 \times 10^{-12} \text{ N}$$ in the direction of the incident light.
